title: A Calculator With Precedence

concept.title: Two stacks: values and operators, and a rule about who goes first
body: Now the expression has `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and parentheses. `*` and `/` bind stronger than `+` and `-`, and `/` is the **integer division that truncates towards zero** (`-7 / 2` is `-3`). Use two stacks: one for **numbers** and one for **operators** (and `(`).

Reading left to right: a **number** goes on the number stack. A **`(`** goes on the operator stack. A **`)`** applies operators until the matching `(` is on top, and then removes it. For an **operator** `op`: while the top of the operator stack is an operator with a precedence **greater or equal** to `op` (so that `a - b - c` is evaluated from left to right), apply it first; then push `op`. At the end apply all remaining operators.

body.code:
def apply():                                  # take two numbers and one operator
    b = nums.pop(); a = nums.pop(); op = ops.pop()
    nums.append(a + b if op == "+" else a - b if op == "-" else a * b if op == "*" else trunc_div(a, b))

"+" or "-": while ops and ops[-1] != "(" and prec[ops[-1]] >= prec[op]: apply()

body: Python's `//` rounds towards minus infinity, so for negative results write the division with absolute values and fix the sign: `q = abs(a) // abs(b)`, negative if the signs differ. C++ and Java already truncate towards zero with `/`.

statement: Evaluate an expression with non-negative integers, the operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, parentheses and spaces. The division is an integer division that truncates towards zero. The expression is valid, a divisor is never zero, there is no unary minus (a `-` always has a number or a parenthesis on its left), and every partial value has an absolute value below 10^16.
outputFormat: Print the value of the expression.
constraints: The parentheses are nested at most 1500 levels deep.
hints: Keep a stack of numbers and a stack of operators.
Before pushing an operator, apply the operators on top that have the same or a higher precedence.
At `)` apply operators until `(` is on top. Remember that the division truncates towards zero.

explanation: Numbers and operators are kept on two stacks. Before an operator is pushed, operators of the same or higher precedence on top are applied; `)` applies operators until `(`. Division truncates towards zero.
